analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA temporarily import foreign-made drugs and speed up generics during drug shortages.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a lifesaving prescription drug runs short or has almost no competitors, the FDA would have to allow temporary imports of the same drug from countries like Canada, for up to three years. It would also speed up review of generic applications and inspections for drugs stuck in markets with fewer than five sellers, and require an annual report on how many drugs get imported.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who rely on drugs in chronic shortage — generic injectable medicines like chemotherapy and anesthesia drugs — as well as hospitals and pharmacists struggling to stock them.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to authorize importation of prescription drugs that are facing shortages, if they are marketed in certain foreign countries and have the same active ingredient, starting within 60 days of an application.

Treats drugs in 'marginally competitive markets' (fewer than five approved sellers, approved at least 10 years, expired patents) as being in shortage, triggering importation and expedited generic review and inspections.
Import authority ends after three years or when the shortage resolves, and the FDA may deny imports on safety or effectiveness grounds.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug makers with near-monopolies on old, off-patent drugs, who would face temporary competition from imports; FDA would bear new review workload.

drawbacks.text: The FDA may deny importation only on safety or effectiveness grounds, but foreign versions of U.S.-approved drugs can differ in manufacturing, labeling, and packaging, raising oversight costs and risk if the agency's capacity to vet foreign plants falls short.

Importation is capped at three years and limited to shortage or low-competition drugs, so it does nothing to address the underlying economics — like below-cost reimbursement and thin generic margins — that drive shortages in the first place.
Imported manufacturers would need to seek U.S. generic approval, which could deter some foreign suppliers from participating, limiting the remedy's reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, time-limited fix: it targets the most dangerous kind of shortage — old off-patent drugs with almost no producers — where imports could quickly restore supply. The main cost falls on drugmakers' pricing power, not consumers, though the FDA would need resources to vet foreign plants and the measure doesn't fix the root causes of shortages.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in March 2023, and it never received a markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 16, 2023, and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was recorded; the bill died in committee at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drugmakers that hold dominant positions in old, off-patent drug markets keep their pricing power, since the competition from imports never arrived. Patients relying on shortage-prone drugs saw no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drugmakers with monopoly positions on old drugs

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand FDA importation authority during drug shortages.

for.name: Sens. Lee, Durbin, and Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including two Senate Republicans alongside two Democrats.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill after it was referred.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor time for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a bipartisan core — two Democrats (Klobuchar, Durbin) and two Republicans (Lee, Grassley) — but died without any recorded vote in committee or on the floor.

industries.industry: Drugmakers with dominant share of off-patent drugs
industries.note: The bill treats near-monopoly markets as shortages and forces temporary import competition, undercutting the ability of a handful of producers to keep prices high when supplies run short. Patients pay more and face rationing when these markets fail.

The bill speeds up generic review and inspection, which could help generics get to market faster. But imported competitors could also squeeze margins further in a sector already facing chronic underpricing and exit from low-profit markets.
Shortages of injectable generics force rationing, workarounds, and higher procurement costs; a reliable import channel would ease that burden.
